page7_img_1.png.title: Top-1 precision and accuracy of merge approaches on TypeScript
page7_img_1.png.description: A small table reporting top-1 precision and accuracy (percent) for several merge-resolution approaches evaluated on the TypeScript test set. Row values: line-granularity LM baseline (Precision 3.6, Accuracy 3.1) and DeepMerge (55.0 / 35.1); token-granularity diff3 (82.4 / 36.1); token-granularity LM (49.7 / 48.1), DeepMerge (64.5 / 42.7), and MergeBERT (69.1 / 68.2, shown as best). The table shows that while token-level diff3 has the highest precision when it produces a suggestion, its overall accuracy is low (it often produces no suggestion), whereas MergeBERT achieves the best balance with substantially higher accuracy (68.2%) and the highest token-level neural precision (69.1%), improving over previous neural and structured baselines.

page8_img_fig4.png.title: Pipeline for selecting candidate merge conflicts for the user study
page8_img_fig4.png.description: A left-to-right flowchart showing how candidate merge conflicts were identified for the user study. Open-source repositories are mined to extract branch pairs (red and blue branch icons) and their historical merge resolutions; these merge conflicts and resolutions are fed into MergeBERT which produces ranked resolution suggestions (document icons with incoming arrows). Conflicts for which MergeBERT did not produce a matching resolution in its top-3 suggestions (marked with a black X) are selected and presented via a survey-style interface (right) for developers to evaluate with study questions. The figure summarizes the filter-and-survey pipeline used to collect the 122 real-world conflicts evaluated by participants.

page3_img_1.png.title: Three-panel example of line-level, token-level, and resolved JavaScript merge conflict
page3_img_1.png.description: A three-panel illustration of the same JavaScript merge showing (left) the original diff3 line-level conflict with git markers (<<<<<<< A.js, ||||||| O.js, =======, >>>>>>> B.js), (center) the token-level diff3 alignment, and (right) the final resolved file. The left panel shows the common prefix (y = 9; z = 0), then A’s line "let x = max(y, 11)", the base O’s "var x = max(y, 10)", and B’s "var x = max(y, 12, z)" with the suffix console.log(x). The middle panel shows how token-level merging lifts the non-conflicting tokens (the "let x = max(y," fragment becomes part of the prefix and ")" part of the suffix) and localizes the conflict to the numeric/argument tokens 11, 10, and 12, z. The right panel shows the resolved result "y = 9; z = 0; let x = max(y, 12, z); console.log(x)", demonstrating that the final resolution combines A’s non-conflicting keyword change (let) with B’s token-level argument edit (12, z) — a resolution that is not simply a single whole line from either A or B and illustrates the token-level classification strategy described in the paper.

page5_img_1.png.title: Edit-sequence alignment showing replacement and insertions in token-level merge
page5_img_1.png.description: Three aligned rows illustrate an edit sequence between a base/token pair used by MergeBERT: the top row (o|b) shows the source tokens (x = max ( y , 10 [PAD] [PAD] )), the bottom row (b|o) shows the target tokens after the edit (x = max ( y , 11 , z )), and the middle row (∆bo) shows the edit actions per token. Most positions are '=' indicating unchanged tokens; one position is a '↔' replacement corresponding to 10→11, and two '+' actions indicate inserted tokens (a comma and 'z'); padding tokens are used to align the sequences. This visual demonstrates how the model represents a transformation that both swaps a token value and inserts two tokens to produce the target argument list.

page4_img_1.png.title: MergeBERT multi-input transformer for token-level merge resolution
page4_img_1.png.description: Diagram of the MergeBERT pipeline for resolving a three-way merge conflict. On the left are the three input program versions (A, O, B) and a small example conflict (the line with let x = max(y, ...)), from which token-level pairwise alignments a|o, o|a, b|o, and o|b and edit sequences Δ_ao and Δ_bo are extracted. Each aligned token sequence is embedded with token, position and edit-type embeddings and independently encoded (BERT-style); the four encoded tensors are then aggregated (learnable weights θ_x) into a single hidden state that feeds a classification layer and a resolution-decoding step. The example shows the model selecting the token-level edit from B to produce the final resolved line let x = max(y, 11, z).

page6_img_table_1.png.title: Merge conflict dataset counts by language (development vs test)
page6_img_table_1.png.description: Table listing number of merge-conflict examples per programming language in the development and test splits: C# — 27,874 (dev) and 6,969 (test); JavaScript — 66,573 (dev) and 16,644 (test); TypeScript — 22,422 (dev) and 5,606 (test); Java — 103,065 (dev) and 25,767 (test). The totals sum to approximately 219,934 examples in the development set (~220k) and 54,986 in the test set (~55k), matching the paper’s reported dataset sizes used for finetuning and evaluation. The distribution is imbalanced: Java provides the largest share (≈47% of the development data), JavaScript ≈30%, C# ≈13%, and TypeScript ≈10%.

page7_img_2.png.title: Comparison of MergeBERT, JDIME, and JSFSTMERGE: coverage, precision, accuracy
page7_img_2.png.description: A small table compares tool performance on Java and JavaScript conflicts across three metrics: percentage of conflicts for which the tool produces a resolution, precision (top-1), and accuracy (top-1). For Java, JDIME produces resolutions for 82.1% of conflicts but has low precision (26.3%) and accuracy (21.6%), whereas MergeBERT produces resolutions for 98.9% with much higher precision (63.9%) and accuracy (63.2%). For JavaScript, JSFSTMERGE produces a resolution for only 22.8% of conflicts and attains 15.8% precision and 3.6% accuracy, while MergeBERT produces resolutions for 98.1% with 66.9% precision and 65.6% accuracy. Overall, the table shows MergeBERT achieves substantially higher coverage and correct-resolution rates than the language-specific semi‑structured tools (roughly 2–3× improvement in precision/accuracy).
